edges.description: Cytotoxic agents act on cells traversing S phase and mitosis, so the injury is conditional on the progenitor pool actively cycling.
edges.source: Cytotoxic chemotherapy exposure and hematopoietic progenitor injury

edges.description: Loss of cycling progenitors depletes the granulocytic pool the marrow can produce.
Suppressed granulopoiesis lowers the circulating neutrophil count.
A low neutrophil count raises the risk of infection and febrile neutropenia.

nodes.description: Loss of functional progenitors suppresses bone marrow hematopoietic output. In this entry the suppression is viewed through its effect on granulopoiesis, reducing the marrow's capacity to replace circulating neutrophils.

evidence.reference_title: Marrow adipogenic lineage precursors (MALPs) facilitate bone marrow recovery after chemotherapy.
evidence.snippet: The resultant bone marrow suppression is a major dose-limiting side effect.

nodes.description: Marrow toxicity is not simply a matter of drug reaching the bone marrow: it depends on the haematopoietic stem and progenitor pool being in active cell cycle when the cytotoxic agent arrives. That cell-cycle dependence is what makes the marrow a preferential target, and it is also a pharmacologically addressable step - holding progenitors in G1 for the duration of drug exposure protects them without changing the drug or its dose.

evidence.snippet: trilaciclib induces a transient, reversible G1 cell cycle arrest of proliferating haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in bone marrow, thus protecting them from damage during chemotherapy

nodes.description: Myelosuppressive chemotherapy delivers cytotoxic drugs to the bone marrow, where rapidly proliferating hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells are preferentially injured — the conserved initiating lesion of the myelosuppression module, here viewed through its granulocytic consequence.

nodes.description: Neutropenia impairs host defense, raising the risk of infection and febrile neutropenia — the principal driver of morbidity and mortality and the reason chemotherapy doses are delayed or reduced.

nodes.description: Reduced marrow output lowers the circulating neutrophil count. This node specializes the module's multilineage-cytopenia effector to the neutrophil lineage, the predominant and most clinically consequential cytopenia for many regimens.

evidence.snippet: one of the most common side effects of chemotherapy is myelosuppression, which typically manifests as neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and/or lymphopenia

nodes.description: A short-acting intravenous CDK4/6 inhibitor given before chemotherapy rather than as treatment for established neutropenia. It holds haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in a transient, reversible G1 arrest for the duration of cytotoxic exposure, so the marrow is protected without altering the chemotherapy regimen. Approved in the USA in February 2021 for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer receiving platinum/etoposide or topotecan. This is prophylactic myeloprotection, mechanistically distinct from G-CSF, which accelerates recovery after the injury has occurred.

evidence.snippet: In February 2021, trilaciclib received its first approval in the USA to decrease the incidence of chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression in adult patients when administered prior to a platinum/etoposide-containing regimen or topotecan-containing regimen for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer (ES-SCLC).

evidence.snippet: Trilaciclib clinically and significantly reduced both the duration of severe neutropenia (DSN) in cycle 1, a surrogate for febrile neutropenia (FN) and infections, and the occurrence of severe neutropenia (SN)

evidence.snippet: For those patients in the trilaciclib group who did experience SN, the duration of those events was shorter compared with placebo (median duration of 3 versus 8 days).
